paper.title: Migration for co‐residence among long‐distance couples: The role of local family ties and gender
paper.code_data_availability: The data that support the findings of this study are available from Statistics Denmark. Restrictions apply to the availability of these data, which were used under license for this study.

linkages: two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are linked as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address
individuals are linked to non‐resident parents, siblings and children, and the straight‐line distance between the centre points of their parishes of residence is computed
each partner is linked to the characteristics of his or her municipality of origin from StatBank Denmark

sample.universe: opposite‐sex couples in the Danish population register, both partners aged 18–70, entering co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017
sample.unit_of_observation: couple (co‐residence event); about 4.5% of men and women contribute more than one event

living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), which implies that at least one partner moved 30 km or more

sample.n_observations: 72,659 couples and co‐residence events after excluding missing location/distance data; Table 3 reports N = 72,557 long‐distance couples (after excluding the 102 couples with a resident child over 35)

construction_notes: The dependent variable is the woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence; the man's share is its complement.

A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t with that of 1 January of year t + 1; multiple moves within a year are not observed and any distance between the two addresses is assumed to result from a single move.

Distances are straight‐line distances between the centre points of parishes (2,083 parishes in 2018, median population 1,100), computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017); road‐network distances and exact address coordinates were not available.
'Living nearby' for family members is operationalized as living less than 5 km away.
Distance to the workplace is a ready‐made Statistics Denmark variable and is a road‐distance, unlike the paper's other distance measures.

Independent variables are measured before a potential move and updated annually — most on 1 January, distance to the workplace on the last working day of November of the year before, and educational attainment on 1 October of the year before.
Income is the disposable personal income of the previous year, net of interest and taxes, in DKK/10,000; the male income advantage is the man's share in total couple income minus the woman's share.
Base levels for the categorical variables are the categories indicating the absence of a local tie.
In Table 5 the coefficients in the man's column are the inverse (opposite sign) of those estimated on the woman's share; Table 6 reports effects on the woman's share throughout.

claims.statement: Among long‐distance couples entering co‐residence in Denmark, 'A school‐going child (age 6–17)' (resident child(ren); reference category: none) is associated with a lower share of the total distance moved by both partners that is moved by the woman, holding the other covariates of model 2 constant.

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: Categorical indicator of children born before the current relationship who live in the same household, distinguishing those of school‐going age (6–17), a child aged <6 with no school‐going child, and only children aged 18–35; reference category: no resident children. Couples were excluded if one or both partners had a resident child over 35 years old.

timing.value: measured before a potential move and updated annually, on 1 January of the year of entry into co‐residence

outcome.label: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co‐residence

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); yearly address data, distances computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017)

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

timing.value: the year of entry into co‐residence (address on 1 January of year t vs 1 January of year t + 1)

units.value: share of the total distance moved by both partners (the outcome is a proportion between 0 and 1)

magnitude.interpretation: the paper calls this 'a large effect'

estimand.target_population: opposite‐sex long‐distance couples in Denmark (both partners aged 18–70, living 60 km or more apart) who entered co‐residence between 2009 and 2017
estimand.time_horizon: the year of entry into co‐residence (1 January of year t to 1 January of year t + 1)

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.
subgroups_defined: which partner has the tie or resource: he only / she only / both / neither
population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

ambiguities: Tables 4–6 print no N; the N recorded is the long‐distance‐couple N of Table 3 (72,557).

The paper reports associations from an observational multi‐level model and makes no claim of exogenous variation; 'selection_on_observables' records its extensive conditioning, not a causal identification claim by the authors.
baseline_mean is the sample mean of the dependent variable among long‐distance couples (Table 3), expressed as a proportion; no reference‐category mean of the outcome is printed.
The paper links this coefficient to its stated hypothesis H2.

evidence.how: Table 3 reports the average female share in the total distance moved by both partners as 54.2% among long‐distance couples; expressed as a proportion (0.542) to match the units of the dependent variable, which is a share between 0 and 1. This is the sample mean of the outcome, not a reference‐category mean: the paper prints no mean of the outcome for the reference category of this variable.
The paper prints no standard deviation of the dependent variable; Table 4 reports variance components of the null model but no outcome SD.
The table prints a coefficient and a standard error only; no confidence interval is printed anywhere in the paper.

Tables 4–6 print no N. The paper reports a final data set of 72,659 couples and co‐residence events and a further exclusion of 102 long‐distance couples with a resident child over 35; 72,659 − 102 = 72,557, which is the N printed for long‐distance couples in Table 3.

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.

population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: The shortest road‐distance between the individual's home address and workplace address (<10 km, 10–49 km, ≥50 km, unknown), measured on the last working day of November of the year before. timing.value: measured before a potential move and updated annually, on 1 January of the year of entry into co‐residence

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); yearly address data, distances computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017)

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

units.value: share of the total distance moved by both partners (the outcome is a proportion between 0 and 1)

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

definition.value: The shortest road‐distance between the individual's home address and workplace address (<10 km, 10–49 km, ≥50 km, unknown), measured on the last working day of November of the year before. definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

claims.statement: Among long‐distance couples entering co‐residence in Denmark, 'Owner‐occupied' (housing tenure; reference category: rental housing) is associated with a lower share of the total distance moved by both partners that is moved by the woman, holding the other covariates of model 2 constant.

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: Whether the individual lives in rental housing, in an owner‐occupied home, or tenure is unknown. Who owns the home is unknown; for those living with a parent the classification is likely indicative of parental rather than individual homeownership.

timing.value: measured before a potential move and updated annually, on 1 January of the year of entry into co‐residence

outcome.label: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co‐residence

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); yearly address data, distances computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017)

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

timing.value: the year of entry into co‐residence (address on 1 January of year t vs 1 January of year t + 1)

units.value: share of the total distance moved by both partners (the outcome is a proportion between 0 and 1)

estimand.target_population: opposite‐sex long‐distance couples in Denmark (both partners aged 18–70, living 60 km or more apart) who entered co‐residence between 2009 and 2017
estimand.time_horizon: the year of entry into co‐residence (1 January of year t to 1 January of year t + 1)

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.
subgroups_defined: which partner has the tie or resource: he only / she only / both / neither
population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: Dummy variable indicating whether the individual lives in his or her municipality of birth.

timing.value: measured before a potential move and updated annually, on 1 January of the year of entry into co‐residence

outcome.label: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co‐residence

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); yearly address data, distances computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017)

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

timing.value: the year of entry into co‐residence (address on 1 January of year t vs 1 January of year t + 1)

units.value: share of the total distance moved by both partners (the outcome is a proportion between 0 and 1)

estimand.target_population: opposite‐sex long‐distance couples in Denmark (both partners aged 18–70, living 60 km or more apart) who entered co‐residence between 2009 and 2017
estimand.time_horizon: the year of entry into co‐residence (1 January of year t to 1 January of year t + 1)

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.
subgroups_defined: which partner has the tie or resource: he only / she only / both / neither
population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: No exogenous variation is used: the paper compares couples who differ in both partners' observed local family ties, resources and municipality‐of‐origin characteristics measured before the move, within a cross‐classified multi‐level model.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the covariates included in the model (both partners' local family ties, resources and other local ties, and both partners' municipality‐of‐origin characteristics) and on the cross‐classified municipality random intercepts, the association between the characteristic and the share in the distance moved is not confounded by unobserved factors.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.

key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper offers no test of this; it states only that the model accounts for other relevant factors and that unobserved variables introduce further potential error.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: These findings are consistent with those of prior research on moving for co‐residence (Brandén & Haandrikman, 2018; Schnor & Mulder, 2018).

claims.statement: Among long‐distance couples who moved at the start of co‐residence, the median distance moved is larger for women (89.7 km) than for men (84.4 km).

treatment.label: Sex of the partner (woman vs man) within the opposite‐sex couple

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: The couple's two partners, distinguished as the female and the male partner; the Danish population register classifies two people of the opposite sex sharing an address as a co‐residing couple.

timing.value: fixed characteristic, observed at the start of co‐residence

outcome.label: Median distance moved (km) — movers only

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); yearly address data, distances computed on geodatabase Map10 (2017)

definition.value: The median straight‐line distance moved at the start of co‐residence, among those who moved, computed between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

timing.value: the year of entry into co‐residence (address on 1 January of year t vs 1 January of year t + 1)

units.value: kilometres

magnitude.interpretation: the paper states that the median moving distance is higher for women than for men

estimand.target_population: opposite‐sex long‐distance couples in Denmark (both partners aged 18–70, living 60 km or more apart) who entered co‐residence between 2009 and 2017
estimand.time_horizon: the year of entry into co‐residence (1 January of year t to 1 January of year t + 1)

population.description: Opposite‐sex couples registered in the Danish population registers in which both partners were aged 18–70, who entered co‐residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who were living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence.
subgroups_defined: which partner has the tie or resource: he only / she only / both / neither
population.selection: Two people of the opposite sex sharing an address are classified as a co‐residing couple if they are not family members, their age difference is less than 16 years and no other adults live at the same address; the analysis is restricted to couples living 60 km or more apart before co‐residence (about 15% of all new couples), excludes observations with missing location and/or distance data, and excludes couples in which a partner had a resident child over 35 years old.

identification.source_of_variation: None: this is a description of observed moving patterns among the selected long‐distance couples.

key_assumptions.assumption: Any move observed between 1 January of year t and 1 January of year t + 1 is a single move related to the event of entering co‐residence.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as an assumption; the paper notes in its limitations that it cannot be certain that someone's motive for migration was to start co‐residence, and that it cannot identify multiple moves within a year.

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on entering co‐residence between 2009 and 2017 while living 60 km or more apart, so that at least one partner had to migrate; results describe this selected set of couples.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The selection is described in the data section; sensitivity analyses use 80 km and 100 km thresholds and report very similar results.

implies_edges.from: selection into the sample (long‐distance couples, ≥60 km apart, entering co‐residence 2009–2017)
implies_edges.to: Median distance moved (km) — movers only

key_assumptions.assumption: The study population, although it is the full register population, can be treated as a sample from a larger theoretical 'super‐population', which is what makes significance testing meaningful here.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued explicitly in the analytical strategy section, citing Thygesen and Ersbøll (2014).

key_assumptions.assumption: Register‐based identification of co‐residing opposite‐sex pairs as couples is accurate enough that the remaining misclassification (notably of students and young people sharing housing) does not bias the estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sensitivity analyses restricted to those aged 30+ and non‐students gave otherwise similar results.

threats_discussed: misclassification of roommates or friends as co‐residing couples
yearly data cannot identify multiple moves within one year, which may overestimate the average distance moved
straight‐line distances may not reflect travel distance, particularly around the islands of Denmark
robustness_checks: sensitivity analyses using distance thresholds of 80 km and 100 km instead of 60 km
analyses restricted to those aged 30+ and non‐students
sensitivity check selecting only the first co‐residence event observed since 2009

claims.statement: In the constant‐only cross‐classified model, variation between couples accounts for about 97% of the total variation in the woman's share in the distance moved, leaving only about 3% to the partners' municipalities of origin.

treatment.label: Partners' municipalities of origin before co‐residence (geographical context)

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code); municipality of residence before co‐residence

definition.value: The woman's and the man's municipality of residence before co‐residence, entered as two cross‐classified higher‐level classifications with random intercepts plus a random interaction between the two; Denmark comprises 98 municipalities.

timing.value: municipality of residence before entry into co‐residence

outcome.label: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co‐residence (variance decomposition)

register_source.value: Danish population register (the paper names no DST register code)

definition.value: The female partner's share in the total distance moved by both partners in the year of entry into co‐residence (e.g. if she moved in with him and they lived 70 km apart, Y = 70/(70 + 0) = 1); the male partner's share is the complement. A move is identified by comparing the registered address on 1 January of year t and of year t + 1, and its distance is approximated by the straight‐line distance between the centre points of the parishes of the previous and the new address.

timing.value: the year of entry into co‐residence (address on 1 January of year t vs 1 January of year t + 1)

units.value: proportion of the total variance in the woman's share in the distance moved

magnitude.interpretation: the paper concludes that geographical context seems to play a modest role
